newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Burundi ruler says sanctions eased on his country.
newsitem.headline: Burundi ruler says sanctions eased on his country.

text.p: Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya said African regional leaders eased sanctions on Wednesday against his ethnically torn country to encourage the peace process.

Leaving a one-day summit on sanctions in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha, Buyoya told reporters the leaders agreed to lift sanctions on food, agricultural products, educational material, medicine and construction materials.
"It has been decided to lift sanctions on all food items. Sanctions have been lifted which concern the ordinary people," said Buyoya, who then listed categories exempt from sanctions.

"I think it's a very important step. Our expectations were higher. However I think it is an encouraging signal to go forward with the peace process," added the Tutsi retired army officer who seized power in an army coup on July 25 last year.
It was a diplomatic victory for Buyoya at the first summit on sanctions he was invited to attend. He was welcomed as "president" to the talks by host Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa.
Regional leaders imposed sanctions on landlocked Burundi on July 31 last year, demanding Buyoya return it to constitutional rule and open immediate unconditional talks with Hutu rebels.
Buyoya has said he is ready for unconditional talks but has not begun them. Negotiations are opposed by hardline members of the Tutsi-dominated army and former military ruler Jean-Baptiste Bagaza.
Addressing leaders and Buyoya at the summit in the Arusha conference centre, Mkapa said: "For us today to focus entirely on reviewing sanctions is to miss the forest for the trees.

"Sanctions were imposed only as a tool for a specific purpose. Sanctions were only intended to open the ears, eyes and minds of all stake-holders in Burundi to avoid the path of mutual annihiliation."

The summit was attended by Mkapa, Moi, the prime ministers of Rwanda and Ethiopia, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, Zambian President Frederick Chiluba, Organisation of African Unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim and former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, international mediator on Burundi.
Buyoya, a Tutsi, and the army ousted Burundi's civilian Hutu president in the coup last year but argued sanctions only hurt the poorest and were fuelling Tutsi extremism in his country.
But in his latest report, U.N. Special Rapporteur for Human Rights Paulo Pinheiro said in February "there is no sign of the beginnings of a Burundi strategy for peace and reconciliation".
The report added that while the government said it wanted to hold talks with all parties to the conflict "it's actual political decisions seem, on the contrary, to be war-oriented".
More than 150,000 people have been killed in massacres and fighting between the army and rebels since the killing by soldiers of Burundi's first elected Hutu president in 1993.
Hutu rebels led by former Burundi minister Leonard Nyangoma took issue with Buyoya's trip to Tanzania, saying he had not met conditions set by the heads of state for sanctions to be lifted.
Preliminary findings of a U.N.-funded study of the sanctions issued on Tuesday found no hard evidence they had succeeded in their political aims while smuggling was weakening their impact.

"While it is possible that concessions by the regime may, in part, be the result of prolonged sanctions, there is no concrete evidence that sanctions have been (politically) successful," said researchers from Brown University in the United States.
